strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear illustration of ICL failure in smaller LMMs (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental methodology with multiple baselines, ablations, robustness analysis, and task decomposition
Consistent improvements with FT-based adaptation on some tasks (Open-MI: 77.9% vs 64.5%; Operator Induction: 47.7% vs 30.9%)
Desirable monotonic improvement property as number of shots increases
Extensive reproducibility details and implementation documentation in appendix
Strong performance on fast concept binding task compared to LLaVA-OneVision models
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (attention-mapper from Najdenkoska et al., MAML from Finn et al., soft prompts from Lester et al.) without significant innovation or novel insights
Confounded experimental design: major architectural change (LLaVA Vicuna-7B → Qwen2.5-7B) lacks ablation, making it unclear whether improvements come from the method or the better LLM
Critical practical limitation: Figure 23 shows ~5× test-time computational overhead compared to ICL, directly contradicting the few-shot learning efficiency paradigm
Mixed task-dependent results: underperformance on Operator Induction ICL (9.6% vs 20.6%), marginal gains on CLEVR and TextOCR, inconsistent across tasks
Narrow evaluation scope: limited to 4 single-image VQA tasks from VL-ICL Bench; no evaluation on standard benchmarks (VQAv2, OKVQA); multi-image scenarios excluded
Test-time adaptation conflates training and inference: requires gradient-based adaptation on support set with potential validation data contamination from training distribution
Hand-curated mathematical reasoning data not part of original datasets; using Qwen2.5-VL-32B as judge introduces model bias
Insufficient interpretability: no visualization of learned prompts; limited analysis of why MAPD works mechanistically
Missing key ablations: no isolated comparison of attention-mapper contribution vs. MAML vs. Qwen2.5 LLM swap
Example similarity dependency: ~4.8-8.6% improvement requires access to similarity information, limiting practical applicability
No statistical significance testing or error bars; appears to be single runs with high variance on some tasks

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly demonstrates non-monotonic ICL performance in smaller LMMs (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple baselines, extensive ablations, robustness testing under image perturbations
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation details, promises to release code
Insightful task decomposition: breaks down Operator Induction into perception, task induction, and reasoning components
Thorough documentation: well-organized appendix with qualitative results and detailed hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (MAML, attention-mapper, soft prompts) in straightforward manner—core components from prior work (Finn 2017, Najdenkoska et al. 2023, Lester et al. 2021)

Unfair experimental comparisons: changes base LLM from Vicuna-7B to Qwen2.5-7B, making it impossible to isolate MAPD's contribution from LLM quality improvement—missing ablation with Qwen2.5 + multi-task learning without MAML
Prohibitive test-time computational cost: requires 30 gradient steps (~5× more compute than ICL), severely limiting practical applicability despite positioning as few-shot adaptation method

Modest improvements over simpler baselines: MAPD vs Multi-TaskPD shows only 1-3.5% gains (e.g., 2.6% on Operator Induction); added MAML complexity poorly justified; improvements may lack statistical significance on small test sets (60-200 examples)
Limited task coverage: only single-image VQA tasks from one benchmark; explicitly excludes multi-image scenarios; tasks are relatively simple

Dataset-specific tuning concerns: hand-curated detailed reasoning steps added to training data for math reasoning evaluation (Figure 15)—appears to optimize for specific task rather than general few-shot learning

Experimental issues: uses different model (Qwen-2.5-VL-32B) as judge; no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; hyperparameter sensitivity evident (Table 5 shows 0.6-1.0 learning rates across methods)
Competitive simple baselines: In-ContextPD achieves 64.5% on Open-MI ICL (nearly matches MAPD's 77.9% FT) and outperforms MAPD on CLEVR ICL, questioning whether MAML complexity is justified
Narrow scope and generalization: evaluation limited to vision tasks only; no evidence of transfer to other domains; restricted to single-image scenarios

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Figure 1 compellingly demonstrates ICL failure in smaller LMMs, with clear intuition about image embedding information overload
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple baselines, thorough ablations (prompt scaling, task decomposition, robustness to perturbations), detailed convergence analysis
Strong empirical results: 21.2% average improvement over ICL with monotonic scaling—key advantage over baseline; robust to image perturbations (1.3% drop vs. 7.0% average)
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, full algorithm, training procedures, computational requirements, and code release promised
Thoughtful analysis: Operator Induction decomposition (Figure 3b) reveals MAPD excels at task induction/reasoning; similarity-based example selection study (Figure 4) shows important insights
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Combines existing techniques (first-order MAML, prompt tuning, attention mechanisms from Najdenkoska et al. 2023); primarily an engineering contribution rather than algorithmic innovation

Confounded architectural changes: Replacing Vicuna-7B with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct makes it unclear whether improvements come from MAPD vs. the superior LLM; main results don't cleanly isolate MAPD's contribution

Significant test-time computational overhead: ~5x TFLOPs compared to ICL (Figure 23) due to 30 gradient steps; acknowledged but unresolved, limiting practical deployment in resource-constrained settings

Narrow evaluation scope: Only 4 tasks from VL-ICL Bench; no other VQA benchmarks (VQAv2, OK-VQA); single-image only; limited to 7B models; scalability to 13B/70B unknown; acknowledged as 'relatively simple math problems'

Test-time adaptation complexity adds practical overhead: Requires task-specific validation set (10% training data), per-task hyperparameter tuning (Table 5: LR 0.6-1.0), K selection via validation; comparison with ICL is asymmetric
Incomplete ablations: No isolation of attention-mapper vs. MAML vs. both; no analysis of inner loop steps K sensitivity; first-order vs. full MAML comparison absent

Mechanism underexplained: How does attention-mapper specifically extract task-relevant information? No visualization of learned prompts or attention patterns; standard multi-head attention (Eq. 1) difference unclear
Missing analysis of failure modes: In-ContextPD sometimes outperforms MAPD on ICL (Table 1); when/why this occurs is under-discussed; no error analysis or significance testing provided

strengths: Clear problem motivation with compelling evidence (Figures 1-2) that ICL fails in smaller LMMs and that image embedding information is the bottleneck
Comprehensive and well-designed experimental evaluation with thorough ablations across architectures, perturbations, and task variants; results consistently show 21.2% improvement over ICL
Strong empirical results demonstrating robustness: monotonic improvement with shots, parameter efficiency (24M vs 300M for LoRA), and generalization across different LMM configurations
Excellent analysis providing mechanistic insights: attention entropy analysis explains why MAPD outperforms InContextPD; ablations on Operator Induction subtasks demonstrate task understanding
High reproducibility standards with extensive implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, promised code release, and detailed appendix with qualitative results
weaknesses: Severely limited architectural scope: only LLaVA-based models evaluated; unable to test modern large models (LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen-VL) due to computational constraints; Table 13 shows MAPD underperforms these larger models on several tasks
Narrow evaluation domain restricted to single-image VQA on VL-ICL Bench; no evaluation on standard benchmarks (VQAv2, OKVQA); limited generalization evidence beyond specialized tasks
Significant test-time computational overhead (~2x inference cost vs ICL) limits practical deployment in latency-critical scenarios; FLOPs-matched comparison doesn't fully address real-world usability

Incremental technical novelty: combines well-established techniques (MAML from 2017, soft prompts, attention-mapper 'inspired by' prior work); primary contribution is application rather than methodological innovation

Insufficient understanding of when/why MAPD works: 'extraneous information' hypothesis lacks rigorous validation; no analysis of learned soft prompt representations; missing guidance for practitioners on method selection

Meta-task construction not thoroughly validated: random sampling without ablation; no sensitivity analysis to composition; high hyperparameter tuning complexity (grid search over many parameters) limits reproducibility
Core motivation diminishes as field scales: addresses limitations of smaller LMMs, but larger models where ICL works better are becoming standard; unclear long-term relevance
